title: De altitudine columnarum sub proprio pondere corruentium

deep.reconstruction:
Context. E510 treats the buckling of a heavy column (weight M, length b, flexural rigidity Ekk). On the previous page Euler set up global equilibrium. The forces are end reactions A and B, a uniformly distributed horizontal load C dx/b, and the weight M distributed as M dx/b. This gave A = C/2 + Mg/b and B = C/2 - Mg/b, where g = (1/b)∫y dx.

This page. Euler cuts the column at an arbitrary point Y, with AX = x and XY = y, and treats Y as fixed. He then computes the bending moment about Y of all forces acting on the segment AY. A running element Uu has coordinates AT = t and TU = u. Because the deflection is small, the arc element is Uu ≈ dt.

(1) The end reaction A contributes the moment Ax.

(2) The element carries a horizontal force UP = C dt/b. Its lever arm about Y is (x - t), so its moment is C(x - t)dt/b. Integrating from 0 to t gives (Ct/b)(x - t/2). Setting t = x gives the total Cx²/(2b), acting clockwise ('dextrorsum').

(3) The element also carries a vertical force UQ = M dt/b. Its horizontal lever arm is QY = y - u, so its moment is M(y - u)dt/b, acting in the same sense as Ax. The integration is completed on the next page: M/b (yt - ∫u dt) becomes M/b (xy - ∫y dx) = (M/b)∫x dy, by parts with y(0) = 0.

The next page combines these moments: Ax + (M/b)∫x dy - Cx²/(2b) = Ekk/r. With 1/r ≈ -y'' this becomes a linear integro-differential equation, the classical small-deflection moment balance for a column under distributed axial load plus lateral load. This is the equation whose treatment in E510 is historically discussed as leading Euler to a problematic or paradoxical conclusion. Greenhill's 1881 Bessel-function solution is often cited as giving the correct critical height.
errors: No mathematical error on this page. The lever arms, the integral (Ct/b)(x - t/2) and the total Cx²/2b are all correct. The following integration by parts on the next page, xy - ∫y dx = ∫x dy, is also correct given y = 0 at A.

ideas.what: Bending moment at a section obtained by integrating the moments of distributed lateral and axial (gravity) loads acting on the cut-off segment, using the small-deflection approximation ds ≈ dt.
ideas.modern_name: Section-moment (free-body) method for beam-columns; Euler–Bernoulli moment balance M = EI/r
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler, and Jakob/Daniel Bernoulli for the elastica moment law
ideas.where_published: Euler, Methodus inveniendi (1744) Additamentum I; Sur la force des colonnes (E238, 1759); E508–E510 (1780)

ideas.what: Moment of the distributed self-weight about a section, written as (M/b)∫x dy via integration by parts.
ideas.modern_name: Axial distributed-load (P-delta) term in the heavy-column buckling equation
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E510), later Greenhill (1881) for the correct critical-height solution
ideas.where_published: E510 itself; discussed in Truesdell, Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies (Opera omnia II.11.2)

deep.surprise_reason: This page is routine statics: elementary moment integrals feeding the well-known E510 equation. Its history is already documented by Truesdell and in the heavy-column literature.
transcription_corrections: Long-s readings like 'refpectu', 'eft', 'fumma' should be read as 'respectu', 'est', 'summa'. The mathematics in the transcription matches the image: UP = C dt/b, UQ = M dt/b, moment C(x-t)dt/b, integral (Ct/b)(x - ½t), total ½Cxx/b, and M(y-u)dt/b.
